headline: Ryokō is literally “to travel + to walk”, from Middle Chinese 旅行.
Iriguchi is 入り + 口, and kuchi changes to guchi by rendaku.
Kumoru is the noun 雲 (kumo, “cloud”) plus the verb suffix る (-ru): cloud, made into a verb.
Atama has an unknown derivation, with theories like heaven (a) plus ball (tama).
Han is from Middle Chinese 半 (MC panH).
Sukunai is possibly related to 少し (sukoshi), and possibly cognate with the ku in 幾 (iku).
Warui is from classical わろし (waroshi); compare まるい (marui) from まろし (maroshi).
Ōkii went opoki → oɸoki → oɸokiki → owokiː → oːkiː, and appears in the Muromachi period.
Miru is cognate with 目 (me, “eye”) and first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Ten is from Middle Chinese 點 (MC temX, “point”).
Shichi is from Middle Chinese 七 (MC tshit).
Semai was originally sebashi, before it became semashi and then lost its medial k.
Mizu is possibly cognate with 瑞 (mizu, “freshness, youth”).
Dōbutsu is from Middle Chinese 動物.
Shitsurei is literally “lose, loss + propriety”, probably from Middle Chinese 失禮.
Mainichi is 毎 (mai-, “each; every”) plus 日 (nichi, jitsu, “day”).
Oya may be cognate with the verb 老ゆ (oyu, “to become old”), from the idea of one's elders.
Toshi originally referred to grain, particularly rice, and by extension the year's harvest.
Yasui first appears in the Kojiki spelled 夜須 (yasu), and is cognate with 休む (yasumu, “to rest”).
Yowai was 弱し in Old Japanese, and a king's name varies between 目弱王 and 眉輪王.
Shiro is the standalone apophonic form of shira, from Proto-Japonic *siro.
Mono is attested in the Kojiki, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *mənə.
Akanbō is attested from the 19th century, shifted from earlier 赤坊 (akabō): 赤 (aka, “red”) plus 坊 (-bō, “little”).
Isshōkenmei comes from 一所懸命 (isshokenmei), which referred to samurai risking their life to defend inherited territory.
Naraberu is the lower monograde shift of 並ぶ (narabu), attested as early as the Man'yōshū of 759 CE.
Hanashi is Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *panas-.
Furui is derived from the verb 旧る (furu, “to age”) plus し (-shi), an adjective-forming suffix.
Hazukashii went padukasiki → ɸadukaɕiki → ɸadukaɕiː → ɸad͡zukaɕiː → hazukaɕii.
Kesshite is from the conjunctive form of the verb 決する (kessuru, “to decide”).
Hikōjō is 飛行 (hikō, “aviation”) plus 場 (-jō, “place”).
